title: Normality (N)

references.label: General microbiology/quantitative methods references (ASM, FDA BAM)

explanation: Normality expresses concentration in terms of reactive equivalents rather than moles of whole molecules, accounting for how many equivalents (e.g. replaceable H+ ions in an acid, or electrons in a redox reaction) each mole of solute contributes to a given reaction. It is most often encountered in titration and acid/base contexts where the number of reactive equivalents per molecule differs from one (e.g. sulfuric acid, which has 2 equivalents of H+ per mole).

variables.meaning: Number of equivalents contributed per mole of solute for the reaction in question (a dimensionless whole number specific to the solute and reaction type)

workedExample.scenario: A 1 M solution of sulfuric acid (H2SO4), which contributes 2 equivalents of H+ per mole.

commonMistakes: Treating normality as interchangeable with molarity for any solute — they are only numerically equal when n = 1.
Using the wrong equivalent count for a given reaction context; the same solute can have a different 'n' depending on whether it is acting as an acid, a base, or a redox reagent.
